title: How to Finance an ADU in California
description: Accessory dwelling units are booming in California. Compare the main ways to finance an ADU, from HELOCs to renovation loans, and how rental income can help.
image_alt: A modern brick house with a large green lawn

faq.q: What's the most common way to pay for an ADU?
faq.a: Many homeowners use home equity through a HELOC, home equity loan, or cash-out refinance. Renovation and construction loans are other options, especially when equity is limited.

faq.q: Can ADU rental income help me qualify for a mortgage?
faq.a: In some cases, yes. FHA updated its policy in 2023 to allow certain ADU rental income, and some other programs and lenders have their own rules. Requirements vary.

faq.q: Do I need permits before financing an ADU?
faq.a: Yes. Lenders and appraisers generally need a permitted, legal unit, and most renovation or construction loans require plans and permits as part of the process.

body_html:
California has spent years making it easier to build accessory dwelling units, the backyard cottages, garage conversions, and attached units often called granny flats. Homeowners build them for aging parents, adult children, rental income, or simply more space. The question I hear most isn't whether to build one. It's how to pay for it.

Here's a practical look at the main financing paths and how to choose between them.

Why ADUs make sense for many homeowners

  • Multigenerational living: keep family close while giving everyone privacy
  • Rental income: help offset your own housing costs
  • Property value: a permitted, well-built ADU can add usable square footage
  • Flexibility: a home office today, a rental tomorrow, a place for family later

State law has steadily expanded where and how ADUs can be built, and the California Department of Housing and Community Development publishes an ADU handbook and resources. Your city's planning department will have the specific local rules.

The main ways to finance an ADU

OptionHow it worksBest when
HELOCDraw funds as construction progresses; first mortgage stays putYou have equity and want flexibility
Home equity loanLump sum with fixed paymentsYou know the full cost up front
Cash-out refinanceReplace your mortgage with a larger oneRefinancing also makes sense on its own
Renovation loanFinancing based partly on the home's value after improvementsEquity today is limited but the finished value supports the loan
Construction loanFunds released in draws during the buildLarger detached projects with a builder
Cash or savingsNo new debtYou have the funds and still keep reserves

If your current mortgage has favorable terms, a HELOC or home equity loan often makes more sense than a cash-out refinance, because you keep your first mortgage untouched. I explain that trade-off in cash-out refinance vs. HELOC.

Renovation loans: building on future value

Renovation loan programs can base the loan amount partly on the home's expected value after the work is complete. That can help homeowners who haven't built enough equity yet. These loans involve more steps: approved contractors, detailed plans and bids, inspections, and funds disbursed as work is completed. They take more coordination but can open the door when other options fall short.

Using ADU rental income to qualify

For buyers purchasing a home that already has a permitted ADU, rental income from the unit can sometimes count toward qualifying. FHA expanded its policy in 2023 through Mortgagee Letter 2023-17 to recognize certain ADU rental income on single-family properties. Other loan programs and lenders have their own rules and limits, so this is a conversation to have early.

Budgeting the full project

ADU costs go beyond construction. Plan for:

  • Design, engineering, and permit fees
  • Utility connections and any required upgrades
  • Site work, especially for detached units
  • Impact or school fees, which vary by city and unit size
  • A contingency for surprises, because there are always surprises
  • Higher property taxes on the added value and increased insurance

Steps to get started

  1. Check local rules for setbacks, size limits, and parking in your city.
  2. Get a rough estimate from a designer or builder who specializes in ADUs.
  3. Review your equity with your loan officer to see which financing paths fit.
  4. Compare options side by side, including total cost and payment.
  5. Line up financing before you sign a construction contract, so your timeline and budget are realistic.
The right ADU financing depends less on the project and more on your current mortgage, your equity, and how you plan to use the unit.

Working with your contractor and lender together

ADU projects go smoothest when your builder and loan officer talk early. Lenders offering renovation or construction financing often require detailed bids, licensed and insured contractors, a draw schedule, and inspections before funds are released. A builder experienced with financed projects will know how to provide that paperwork and how to schedule draws around construction milestones, which keeps the project from stalling while you wait on funding.

Questions to ask before you choose financing

  1. How much equity do I have today, and what will the finished home be worth?
  2. Do I want to keep my current first mortgage as is?
  3. Will construction costs come in stages or all at once?
  4. Do I plan to rent the ADU, and do I want that income documented for future financing?
  5. What happens to my budget if the project runs over?

Your answers usually point clearly toward one or two options. Bring them to your loan officer along with your builder's estimate, and you can compare real numbers side by side. The goal is a financing plan that's in place before construction starts, so the project never pauses waiting on money.

And plan for life after construction: a new unit means new insurance needs, possibly a reassessment of property taxes on the added value, and, if you rent it, landlord responsibilities and local rental rules.

The takeaway

An ADU can be one of the most valuable improvements a California homeowner makes, whether for family or income. Start with local rules and a realistic budget, then match the financing to your situation: equity-based options if you have them, renovation or construction loans if you don't. I'm happy to look at your current loan and equity and map out which paths make sense.
